Our numbers lean slightly more toward Texas Tech than the market, largely because Arizona State may have trouble sustaining drives. We rate Texas Tech among the nation’s best at preventing scoring opportunities and defending the run, while Arizona State has struggled in both areas. The Sun Devils converted only 29.6 percent of their third downs through four games, and their rushing average had fallen from 193.62 yards per game in 2025 to 149.0. We are not reacting to one recent result; the broader efficiency profile creates the concern.

The other side of the matchup also favors Texas Tech. Our numbers show a significant advantage for its offense in creating scoring opportunities against Arizona State’s defense. The Sun Devils entered the season with four new starters in the secondary and allowed 15 plays of at least 20 yards through four games. That gives Texas Tech a plausible route to separation, but the market is already accounting for most of it.

For us, that last point determines the decision. We see football reasons to favor Texas Tech more than the market does, but the disagreement is too narrow to create enough value at the available price. The matchup supports our lean, not a wager.

The useful question is whether Arizona State can turn completions into drive-changing gains before Texas Tech ends possessions. If Texas Tech contains that element, our projected game script becomes much easier to reach.

The concern for us is whether Syracuse can prevent Louisville from controlling the game on the ground. Our longer-run metrics give Louisville a substantial advantage in rushing efficiency, and that could create repeated scoring opportunities while limiting Syracuse's possessions. Syracuse held New Hampshire to 60 rushing yards, but one opener does not erase the broader concern. We can see a path for Syracuse to remain competitive through Angeli and the passing game, but the price does not give us enough separation from our expectation to make this a wager.

We saw Syracuse's rebuilt front produce five sacks in the opener—one-quarter of its entire 2025 total—but run defense is the more important test here, and our numbers still make it the clearest pressure point.

That short sample is not proof, but it illustrates how LSU can control field position and create separation.

The uncertainty comes on the other side. LSU has played at high volume and converted 19 of 33 third downs, but its scoring-opportunity creation has not been especially strong in our numbers. Mississippi State’s ability to prevent those opportunities grades poorly, which helps explain why our model is more favorable toward LSU than the market. Still, LSU committed five turnovers through two games, including four interceptions. That volatility matters when laying a substantial number, and the available price does not give us enough value to move beyond a pass.

The concern for us is Washington State’s offense. Still, Caden Pinnick offers an important counter with his mobility: through four games, he had 201 rushing yards and 13 runs of at least 10 yards.
